query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Elevated temperatures accelerate the formation of a thicker, more Fe3+-rich passive film that acts as a robust barrier against chloride ingress, thereby suppressing corrosion degradation relative to room temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 low-carbon steel with its native surface (and any early passive film) intact.
generation.intervention: Expose identical Q235 steel samples to a controlled chloride-rich corrosive environment (using a moderately concentrated salt solution) at room temperature versus a moderately elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Harsh, chloride-laden environments under static conditions using controlled electrolyte composition, constant pH, and identical exposure durations; tests conducted in the absence of external mechanical disturbances.
generation.structural_mediator: The passive film on the steel surface—specifically its thickness, continuity, and composition (a higher content of Fe2O3/Fe3+ oxides versus less stable oxides).
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, kinetic factors promote rapid oxidation that favors the formation of a denser and more adherent Fe3+-rich oxide (e.g., Fe2O3) layer, enhancing its barrier properties against chloride penetration. In contrast, at room temperature, the native film is thinner and more vulnerable to chloride-induced breakdown, leading to accelerated corrosion once its protective effect is lost.
generation.predicted_outcome: Q235 steel samples exposed at elevated temperature will show lower corrosion rates, higher electrochemical impedance, and a thicker, more uniform Fe3+-rich passive film (as evidenced by surface analysis techniques) compared to room-temperature samples, relative to an untreated reference.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel samples exposed in the same chloride environment at room temperature without any temperature elevation.
generation.boundary: This protective effect is expected only if the chloride concentration and exposure time allow film continuity. If sustained chloride attack or other environmental factors (e.g., pH shifts or mechanical disturbances) overcome the film’s integrity, the advantage at elevated temperature may be negated.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance, the detailed microstructural characteristics of the passive film, and the interplay with other variables (e.g., oxygen availability, pH) remain to be fully elucidated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical sets of pre-exposure Q235 steel samples. Immerse one set in a 3.5% NaCl solution at room temperature (≈25°C) and the other set in the same solution at an elevated temperature (≈60°C). Maintain identical exposure durations and static conditions. At predetermined intervals, measure corrosion kinetics through weight loss tests, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), and potentiodynamic polarization. Conduct surface characterization (SEM, EDS, XPS) to analyze the passive film thickness, continuity, and composition.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance (arc radius and |Z| at low frequency)
Potentiodynamic polarization curves (corrosion current density and potential shifts)
Surface morphology and composition (SEM, EDS, and XPS for Fe oxide phases)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated temperature samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate, enhanced impedance parameters, and demonstrably thicker/more Fe3+-rich passive films compared to the room temperature samples, then the hypothesis that elevated temperature promotes the formation of a superior passive film, leading to corrosion suppression, is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, electrochemical corrosion tests were performed on Q235, X65, X70, and X80 steels embedded in natural saline soil. EIS, PC, SEM, EDS, and XRD were used to investigate the steel corrosion process under laboratory conditions. The main conclusions are as follows: (1) The electrochemical corrosion rate of these four low-carbon steels in saline soil was determined by the rate-controlling step, which varied with the electrode surface state and the surrounding environment. During the corrosion test period, Q235 steel was mainly controlled by mass transfer, while the corrosion of X65 shifted from charge transfer control to mass transfer, co-control, and finally charge transfer control. The corrosion of X70 and X80 shifted from charge transfer control to mass transfer control and then charge transfer control. This indicated that Q235 steel was not able to self-suppress corrosion in the saline soil environment of this experiment. In contrast, the formed corrosion product films on X65, X70, and X80 steel slowed down the corrosion rate to a certain extent. cited_evidence.text: Q235 low-carbon steel has an n value greater than 1 during exposure, indicating a harsh environment for accelerated corrosion. Overall, Q235 low-carbon steel exhibits an accelerating corrosion process. The passivation film provides a good corrosion protective function during the early stage of corrosion. However, during the entire corrosion process, the passivation film falls off during the initial stage, and the surface rust layer on the substrate forms a protective effect, but is relatively weak. In the late stages of corrosion, the protective effect gradually appears. With the prolonged exposure time, the corrosion of Q235 low-carbon steel is likely to reach a relatively stable and slow stage, that is, the corrosion weight loss exponent n decreases below 1. The above analysis verifies the four stages of the accelerated corrosion process of the Q235 steel atmospheric environment. The corrosion weight loss kinetics conforms to the power function change law, and the passivation film on the surface of Q235 low-carbon steel and the matrix rust layer formed after the passivation film rupture have had a good anti-corrosion effect.

In this study, the passivation behavior of Q235 carbon steel at different temperatures of 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C was studied. The specific conclusions are as follows:(1)The passivation process was divided into a rapid passivation phase before 24 h and a stable passivation phase after 24 h. Among them, the early passivation rate was faster at 40 °C and 60 °C, indicating that the increase in temperature accelerated the formation of the passive film.(2)Under different temperature conditions, the passive film products are not the same, and more Fe2O3 is produced with an increase in temperature—which is the main reason for the temperature increases—and the passive film is better and thicker.(3)After passivation, the semiconductor properties of the passive films formed are the same. At a temperature of 20 °C, the capacitance of the passive film after passivation is significantly smaller than that at 40 and 60 °C. As the temperature increases, better passivated films form.
